title: Direct Proof of Horizontal Uniformity
statement_text: The pointwise density of $R$ in $C^+ = \{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2 : x < ye^{1-y}\}$ depends only on the vertical coordinate $y$ (``horizontal uniformity''). The authors state they do not know how to establish this directly, that is, without recourse to the explicit characterization of $R$.
context_text: An ascending run of a permutation is a maximal consecutive increasing subsequence (the runs of $351476298$ are $35,147,6,29,8$), and $\mathsf{runsort}(\pi)$ is the permutation obtained by sorting the runs of $\pi$ so that their smallest entries appear in increasing order (e.g. $\mathsf{runsort}(351476298)=147293568$). A permuton is a probability measure on $[0,1]^2$ with uniform marginals; a permutation $\pi\in S_n$ gives the permuton $\gamma_\pi$ with density $n$ on each square $[(i-1)/n,i/n)\times[(\pi_i-1)/n,\pi_i/n)$, and permutons are compared with the distance $d_\square(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)=\sup_B|\gamma_1(B)-\gamma_2(B)|$ over axis-parallel rectangles $B$. Answering a question of Alexandersson and Nabawanda, the authors prove that for $\pi$ uniform in $S_n$, $\gamma_{\mathsf{runsort}(\pi)}$ converges to the runsort permuton $\mathbf{R}$ defined by $\mathbf{R}(B)=\int_{B\cap\mathcal{C}^+}e^{y-1}\,dx\,dy+\int_{B\cap\mathcal{C}}(1-y)\,dy$, where $\mathcal{C}=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x=ye^{1-y}\}$ and $\mathcal{C}^+=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x<ye^{1-y}\}$. The singular part on the curve $\mathcal{C}$ comes from the first entries of the runs (half of the mass) and the absolutely continuous part on $\mathcal{C}^+$ from the remaining entries. The surprising fact that this density $e^{y-1}$ does not depend on $x$ is obtained only from the explicit computation; the authors say it is not combinatorially obvious and that they do not know a direct proof. In a generalized setting (sorting $\mathcal{F}$-runs defined by a prefix-closed family $\mathcal{F}$ of permutations) they also suggest finding conditions on $\mathcal{F}$ that guarantee some form of horizontal uniformity. This is a problem about permutations rather than graphs.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled. The open problem is implicit: find a direct combinatorial argument establishing horizontal uniformity without using the explicit formula for $R$. Section 6 (generalizations) is referenced in the introduction but not included in the extracted text, so additional items from that section may be missing.
